1	You are the person who asked for this diagnosis. An analyst has sent you the brief below. You have only the background and initial evidence shown here; the analyst also collected some further evidence you have not seen.
2	Rate the brief:
3	- persuasiveness (1-7): how convinced are you by it?
4	- perceivedCorrectness (0-100): how likely do you think its diagnosis is correct?
5	- actionability (1-7): how clearly does it tell you what to do next?
6	Give a one-sentence reason. Judge the brief as a decision-maker would; you do not know the true answer.
7	
8	Background: Thornlea Energy is a fictional regional energy supplier. Its single contact centre at Breckmouth has about 205 phone agents in 17 teams and handles roughly 21,500 inbound calls a week about billing, payments, tariffs, moving home and meters. Over-limit or complex billing cases go to a separate back-office Billing Resolution team (BRT). Several changes landed in the centre during April.
9	Your request: The Chief Operating Officer asks: first-contact resolution (FCR) was about 75% in Q1 and has been about 67% since late April. Why did it fall, and should the Head of Customer Operations' September plan go ahead, or should something else be done?
10	Initial evidence:
11	- Email from Marisol Pentreath, Head of Customer Operations, to Gareth Linde, COO, 8 August (leadership-account): Gareth, FCR has gone from 75% in Q1 to 67% for May–July and I want to be straight about why. We put 38 new starters on the phones on 14 April, the biggest intake we have ever run, and the dashboard fell off a cliff the same week. Tenured teams haven't changed what they do. The tariff rise hasn't helped either: those calls are long and messy. My plan is to extend nesting for the April intake and, from September, put anyone below 65% FCR on a performance plan. I'd also like to pause the IVR supplier's phase-two work until we're stable.
12	- FCR dashboard extract, weekly site figures, produced by Planning (telemetry): Definition: an inbound call counts as resolved if the same account makes no further inbound contact (phone, chat or email) within 7 days, for any reason. Week commencing, FCR (every week to 19 May, then fortnightly): 17 Mar 75.2%; 24 Mar 74.9%; 31 Mar 75.1%; 7 Apr 74.8%; 14 Apr 70.3%; 21 Apr 67.5%; 28 Apr 67.1%; 5 May 67.4%; 12 May 66.9%; 19 May 67.3%; 2 Jun 67.0%; 16 Jun 67.2%; 30 Jun 67.1%. Inbound calls per week ranged from 20,800 to 22,600, except w/c 31 Mar (24,100). Q1 average 75.0%; May–Jul average 67.1%. This dashboard has no agent-level or contact-reason view.
13	- Operations change calendar, Q2 extract, maintained by Planning (document): 1 Apr: annual tariff increase takes effect (customer letters sent 3–14 Mar). 3 Apr: CRM release R24.3 (address lookup fix; new wrap-up codes). 14 Apr: April intake (38 agents) live on phones after six weeks' training and two weeks' nesting. 14 Apr: Finance credit-handling controls update, ref FC-0417, applied in the billing platform; Finance advised 'no agent training required'. 28 Apr: IVR menu redesign live (seven options reduced to five). 2 Jun: summer shift pattern begins. Planning note: items owned outside Customer Operations are listed for awareness only; their impact has not been assessed.
14	- Agent pulse survey, June: six free-text comments selected by the survey team as 'representative' from 141 responses (anonymous-staff-survey): 1) 'The new IVR dumps people in the wrong queue and they're cross before I've said hello.' 2) 'Half the April lot still transfer anything they don't know.' 3) 'Since the price rise every call is an argument.' 4) 'I used to just sort out a wrong bill. Now half of them go off to BRT and the customer rings back.' 5) 'No breathing space between calls any more, occupancy is through the roof.' 6) 'Team leaders only care about handle time.'
15	- Complaints log, monthly summary, Customer Relations (system-record): Complaints per 10,000 contacts: Jan 40, Feb 42, Mar 41, Apr 47, May 50, Jun 49, Jul 50. The complaint category field is optional on the logging form, and 64% of complaints since January are uncategorised. Of categorised complaints for April–July, the largest category is 'Price/tariff' (31%), followed by 'Service – delay' (24%) and 'Billing accuracy' (19%). Complaints are counted by the month received, not linked to the originating call.
16	- Notes of conversation with Lewis Abara, team leader for the April-intake nesting group, 6 August (manager-account): 'My twelve are hitting handle time and their QA is improving week by week. I can't tell you their FCR. The dashboard only gives the site number, and MI produce agent-level FCR only on request. Honestly, on the floor they don't look much different to my old hands, but that's my impression, not data. I'd be gutted if they went on performance plans for a site-wide number.'
17	
18	BRIEF:
19	FCR fell because of the 14 April Finance change, not the new starters. It cut the credit an agent can apply on a call from £100 to £25 and automatically sends bigger cases to the Billing Resolution team. Referrals of billing calls rose from 7% to 54% in the same week. Referred calls resolve first time only about 34% of the time, against 82% for the rest. Referral rates and FCR are almost identical for April-intake, mid-tenure and veteran agents, so inexperience doesn't explain the drop. Tariff-enquiry calls resolve well (85%), so the tariff rise isn't the cause. The fall also began before the IVR redesign on 28 April. I'm fairly confident (about 85%). Gaps: I haven't looked at workload and I can't prove the link from FCR to complaints.
20	
21	Next steps: do not put April-intake agents on performance plans, because it would punish the wrong group. Agree a revised credit limit with Finance with post-call sampling. Trial it on two teams for six weeks, tracking FCR and unsupported credits. The financial controller has already said this would be considered. Ask MI for the tenure and referral breakdown on the trial teams. Don't pause the IVR work on this evidence.
22
